Walmart’s Winning Combo: Thrifty Shoppers and Wary AI Investors
 
Plus, Nvidia’s earnings tailwind, and Anthropic’s multibillionaires
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Investors are exhaling this morning. Nvidia’s blockbuster results and commentary have stopped, for now, the rout in its shares and across the tech sector. Futures are pointing to an upbeat open. Markets are even shrugging off a new round of Iranian attacks in the Gulf region, focusing instead on abundant U.S. inventories. Oil futures are down. Attention now turns to Anthropic’s mega-IPO and its planned trading debut tomorrow.

 

​📈 Follow our live markets data and coverage.

Trading down

 

Even if consumers and the AI trade struggle, Walmart can still be a winner.

 

Despite persistent inflation and gloomy sentiment, consumer spending has been surprisingly resilient this year. There are some signs of cooling, though.

 

On Tuesday, the Commerce Department said retail sales rose 0.2% in October from a month earlier. That was a slowdown from 0.8% in September and also fell short of 0.4% inflation that month.

 

Shoppers may be spending, but they are looking for discounts. Consumers have been trading down at the highest level since 2021, according to a BofA Institute report from earlier this month. Trade-downs are occurring across multiple spending categories, including apparel, dining and groceries.

 

If penny pinching continues, it should be good news for Walmart, which touts “everyday low prices” and reports earnings before the bell Thursday.

 

Walmart’s scale gives it bargaining power to haggle with vendors. And the profit cushion from its growing high-margin streams of revenue—including advertising and its third-party marketplace—allows it to aggressively cut prices.

 

Tariff refunds have helped, too. In its previous quarter, the retailer reported 11,000 price rollbacks, double the typical number, subsidized in part by tariff refunds.

 

Walmart said a large portion of the tariff refund-backed discounts were put in place at the end of its quarter through July. This means some of those sales benefits should show up in its latest quarter. The retailer has already received pretty much all of its $2.9 billion refund and has funneled much of it into rollbacks.

 

Barring big surprises, Walmart is expected to report solid results. Wall Street analysts polled by Visible Alpha think U.S. comparable sales will be up 2.8% in its quarter ended October versus a year earlier.

 

That isn’t the most exciting number, but it would still be a welcome turn. Walmart’s shares took a nosedive after this metric fell short of expectations the last time it reported results.

 

A change in drug-pricing policy was partly to blame back then. But the surprise made investors think twice about Walmart’s valuation, according to Steven Shemesh, an equity analyst at RBC Capital Markets. The stock currently trades at a lofty level of about 40 times forward earnings.

 

But investors may be more willing now to pay a premium for stocks seen as AI-proof.

 

Since early October, there has been a rotation away from AI-related stocks and into defensive sectors like consumer staples. This rotation might not be over just yet, given the Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections and, most recently, the fallout from Nvidia’s scandal.

 

Between consumers’ bargain-hunting tendencies and investors’ cooling sentiment on AI, the winds are blowing in the right direction for Walmart. On Thursday, it will just have to stick the landing.

Colette Kress has a daunting job. She also has a tremendous head start.
